claim: A trained recurrent neural network (RNN) can recognize and transcribe spoken digits into handwritten digits.
source: We show that by tuning the weights of a recurrent neural network (RNN), it can recognize and then transcribe spoken digits.
evidence: Demonstrated through network simulations showing successful transcription of spoken digits 0-9 into handwritten patterns (Figure 1B, Video 1)

claim: Recurrent dynamics in RNNs can encode multiple time-varying sensory and motor patterns as stable neural trajectories.
source: The model elucidates how neural dynamics in cortical networks may resolve three fundamental challenges: first, encode multiple time-varying sensory and motor patterns as stable neural trajectories
evidence: Demonstrated through trajectory analysis showing stable encoding of different digits (Figures 3, 4)

claim: Trained RNNs can generalize across relevant spatial features of stimuli.
source: The model elucidates how neural dynamics in cortical networks may resolve three fundamental challenges: first, encode multiple time-varying sensory and motor patterns as stable neural trajectories; second, generalize across relevant spatial features
evidence: Shown through cross-speaker and cross-utterance generalization performance (Figure 1C)

claim: Temporal invariance in RNNs emerges because recurrent dynamics generate neural trajectories with appropriately modulated angular velocities.
source: third, identify the same stimuli played at different speeds—we show that this temporal invariance emerges because the recurrent dynamics generate neural trajectories with appropriately modulated angular velocities.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of trajectories at different temporal warp factors showing modulated angular velocities (Figures 7, 8)

claim: Many tasks the brain performs are inherently temporal in nature.
source: Many, if not most, of the tasks the brain performs are inherently temporal in nature: from recognizing and generating complex spatiotemporal patterns—such as a phoneme sequence that composes a word—to creating temporal expectations of when an event will occur (Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Nobre et al., 2007; Ivry and Schlerf, 2008; Merchant et al., 2013; Hopfield, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Robust decoding and encoding of time-varying patterns must rely on spatiotemporal dependencies inherent to the pattern.
source: In contrast to the representation of an object in a static image, such as a picture of a face, robust decoding and encoding of a time-varying patterns must rely on the spatiotemporal dependencies inherent to the pattern.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the nature of temporal patterns

claim: Fixed-point attractor theory holds that information is stored as fixed-point attractors in recurrently connected circuits.
source: One highly influential theory in neuroscience holds that information is stored as fixed-point attractors that emerge in the dynamic activity of the brain's recurrently connected circuits (Hopfield, 1982; Hopfield and Tank, 1986; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Wang, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational papers in the field

claim: Fixed-point attractor framework fails to capture the temporal aspect of stored information.
source: Two limitations of this framework are: (1) It fails to capture the temporal aspect of stored information, thus forcing many computational models to 'spatialize' time—that is, they treat the temporal component of time-varying patterns as additional spatial dimensions (Rabiner, 1989; Waibel et al., 1989; Elman, 1990; Hinton et al., 2012; Mnih et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations showing how models spatialize time

claim: Fixed-point attractor framework does not capture temporal invariance in brain processing.
source: (2) it does not capture a fundamental feature of how the brain processes temporal information: temporal invariance. For example, humans readily recognize temporally warped—compressed or dilated—speech or music.
evidence: Based on known human perceptual abilities

claim: Humans readily recognize temporally warped speech or music.
source: For example, humans readily recognize temporally warped—compressed or dilated—speech or music.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of human perception

claim: There is mounting evidence that the ability to tell time on the sub-second scale relies on the dynamics of recurrent neural networks.
source: While the mechanisms that underlie the brain's ability to perform a broad range of spatiotemporal tasks in the sensory and motor domains are not known, there is mounting theoretical and experimental evidence that our ability to tell time on the sub-second scale, and represent time-varying patterns, relies on the inherent continuous dynamics, and computational potential, of recurrent neural networks (Rabinovich et al., 2008; Buonomano and Maass, 2009; Mante et al., 2013; Crowe et al., 2014; Carnevale et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical and experimental studies

claim: The RNN framework alleviates restrictions imposed by traditional discrete-time or fixed-point attractor models by relying on recurrent connections to implicitly maintain an ongoing memory of the pattern.
source: This framework alleviates the restrictions imposed by traditional discrete-time or fixed-point attractor models, by relying on the recurrent connections to implicitly maintain an ongoing memory of the pattern.
evidence: Based on theoretical understanding of RNN dynamics

claim: By tuning the weights within RNN models, it is possible to robustly store and generate complex time-varying motor patterns.
source: Indeed, recent computational studies have established that by tuning the weights within recurrent neural network (RNN) models, it is possible to robustly store and generate complex time-varying motor patterns (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Abbott et al., 2016; Rajan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior computational studies

claim: It remains unknown whether the same RNN approach can be used to robustly discriminate time-varying sensory patterns.
source: What remains unknown is whether the same approach can be used to robustly discriminate time-varying sensory patterns.

claim: Activity in sensory areas is strongly influenced by motor behavior.
source: Neuroscientists have typically distinguished between sensory and motor areas; but it is well established that activity in sensory areas is strongly influenced by motor behavior, and that sensory stimuli can modulate activity in motor areas—furthermore, some brain areas are characterized as being sensorimotor (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Ayaz et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2013; Schneider and Mooney, 2015; Cheung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Sensory stimuli can modulate activity in motor areas.
source: Neuroscientists have typically distinguished between sensory and motor areas; but it is well established that activity in sensory areas is strongly influenced by motor behavior, and that sensory stimuli can modulate activity in motor areas—furthermore, some brain areas are characterized as being sensorimotor (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Ayaz et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2013; Schneider and Mooney, 2015; Cheung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: During sensory processing, network dynamics should primarily be driven by sensory inputs.
source: Computationally, sensory and motor processing are understood to have disparate requirements—during sensory processing, network dynamics should primarily be driven by the sensory inputs
evidence: Based on computational understanding of sensory processing

claim: During motor processing, neural dynamics should be autonomous and driven primarily by recurrent interactions.
source: in contrast, during motor processing neural dynamics should be autonomous and driven primarily by recurrent interactions.
evidence: Based on computational understanding of motor processing

claim: No previous models have shown that the same network can satisfy the requirements for both sensory and motor processing.
source: Indeed, to date, no previous models have shown that the same network can satisfy the requirements for both sensory and motor processing.
evidence: Statement of gap in prior literature

claim: The same RNN can reliably function in both a sensory and motor regime.
source: Here we show that the same RNN can reliably function in both a sensory and motor regime.

claim: The same RNN can convert complex time-varying sensory patterns into motor patterns.
source: Specifically the same RNN can convert complex time-varying sensory patterns into motor patterns—thus performing a transcription task in which spoken digits are identified and read out as 'handwritten' digits.

claim: Temporal invariance is particularly evident in our ability to recognize temporally warped speech or music.
source: This temporal invariance is particularly evident in our ability to recognize temporally warped speech or music (Miller et al., 1984; Sebastián-Gallés et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to perceptual studies

claim: One advantage of storing time-varying patterns as neural trajectories within RNNs is that this strategy naturally accounts for temporal invariance.
source: Our results suggest that one advantage of storing time-varying patterns as neural trajectories within RNNs is that, under the appropriate conditions, this strategy naturally accounts for temporal invariance.

claim: A continuous-time firing-rate RNN with randomly assigned sparse recurrent connections was used in the model.
source: A continuous-time firing-rate RNN with randomly assigned sparse recurrent connections was used (Sompolinsky et al., 1988).

claim: Before training, the network was in a high-gain regime characterized by self-perpetuating and chaotic activity.
source: The strengths of these recurrent connections were initialized to be relatively strong; thus, before training the network was in a so-called high-gain regime (g = 1.6) that is characterized by self-perpetuating and chaotic activity (Materials and Methods).
evidence: Based on known properties of high-gain RNNs with citation

claim: The transcription task is divided into a sensory and a motor epoch.
source: The transcription task is divided into a sensory and a motor epoch.

claim: During the sensory epoch, the RNN is presented with a spoken digit.
source: During the sensory epoch, the RNN is presented with a spoken digit

claim: During the motor epoch, the RNN drives an output pattern transcribing the presented digit via three motor outputs x, y, and z.
source: over the ensuing motor epoch the RNN drives an output pattern transcribing the presented digit via three motor outputs x, y, and z—activity in the x and y units determines the 2D coordinates of a 'pen on paper', while z determines if the 'pen' is in contact with the 'paper' or not.

claim: Successful performance of the transcription task requires the RNN to encode spoken digits with a set of neural trajectories in high-dimensional phase space.
source: Successful performance of this transcription task requires that the RNN: 1) encode spoken digits with a set of neural trajectories in high-dimensional phase space

claim: Successful performance requires the RNN to autonomously generate digit-specific trajectories during the motor epoch.
source: 2) autonomously generate digit-specific trajectories during the motor epoch, in order to drive the digit-specific output patterns

claim: Successful performance requires the RNN to generate trajectories that are stable and invariant to background noise and spatiotemporal variations.
source: and most importantly 3) generate trajectories that are stable so they may encode each digit's sensory pattern, sensory-motor transition, and motor pattern in a manner that is invariant not just to background noise but also to spatiotemporal variations of the spoken digits, including temporal warping.

claim: The RNN was trained using a supervised learning rule in which recurrent units were trained to reproduce their 'innate' patterns of activity.
source: We attempted to satisfy these three conditions by training the RNN using a supervised learning rule, in which the recurrent units were trained to robustly reproduce their 'innate' patterns of activity (Laje and Buonomano, 2013)—that is, those generated in the untrained network—using the recursive-least-squares learning rule (Haykin, 2002; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009).
evidence: Description of training method with citations

claim: The RNN is trained to reproduce one digit-specific 'innate' trajectory in response to all training utterances of a given digit.
source: In essence, the RNN is trained to reproduce one digit-specific 'innate' trajectory in response to all training utterances of a given digit.

claim: The network is trained to reproduce target trajectories regardless of the initial state of the network's units and in the presence of continuous background noise.
source: Furthermore, it is trained to do so regardless of the initial state of the network's units, and in the presence of continuous background noise (Materials and Methods).

claim: Output units are trained after training the RNN to generate handwriting patterns during the motor epoch.
source: Only after training the RNN (recurrent training), are the output units trained to generate the handwriting patterns representing each of the digits during the motor epoch (output training)

claim: The separation of recurrent and output training phases allows for rapid training and retraining of outputs without retraining recurrent weights.
source: this separation of the recurrent and output training phases, while not necessary, allows for rapid training and retraining of the outputs to produce arbitrary motor patterns, without retraining the recurrent weights.

claim: The temporal separation of sensory and motor learning is observed in some forms of sensorimotor learning.
source: Notably, the temporal separation of sensory and motor learning is observed in some forms of sensori-motor learning (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Following training, the network successfully transcribes utterances used during training.
source: Following training, the network successfully transcribes the utterances used during training (marked by asterisks).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B with asterisks marking trained utterances

claim: Performance generalizes to novel utterances and speakers despite significant variations in duration and spatiotemporal structure.
source: More importantly, performance generalizes to novel utterances and speakers in the dataset despite significant variations in the duration and spatiotemporal structure across utterances (Video 1).

claim: A deep convolutional neural network (CNN) was used to rate the performance of trained RNNs.
source: Rather than use a human-based performance measure, we used a standard deep convolutional neural network (CNN) (LeCun et al., 2015) to rate the performance of trained RNNs (Materials and Methods)—i.e., the CNN was used to determine if each 'handwritten' digit was correct or not.

claim: Performance of trained RNNs was 98.7% on a test set of 410 novel stimuli.
source: Performance of trained RNNs was 98.7% on a test set of 410 novel stimuli (Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantitative performance measurement shown in Figure 1C

claim: Untrained RNNs ('reservoir networks') are capable of performing many interesting computations.
source: Since untrained RNNs ('reservoir networks') are in and of themselves capable of performing many interesting computations (Maass et al., 2002; Jaeger and Haas, 2004; Lukoševičius and Jaeger, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to reservoir computing literature

claim: Reservoir networks with only output training achieved 20% performance on the transcription task.
source: The performance was very poor (20%), in large part because during the motor epoch a reservoir RNN is operating in an autonomous mode that is chaotic—making it difficult for the output units to learn to produce the target output patterns.

claim: RNNs trained only during the motor epoch achieved 71% performance.
source: We also examined the effects of training an RNN only during the motor epoch, resulting in a performance of 71%.

claim: A network driven by external inputs can encode sensory stimuli despite a lack of sensory epoch training due to the intrinsic ability of RNNs and the stabilizing influence of external inputs.
source: This significant improvement over the reservoir networks is a consequence of the fact that a network driven by external inputs can encode sensory stimuli despite a lack of sensory epoch training, due to the intrinsic ability of RNNs to encode sensory stimuli and the stabilizing influence of the external inputs (see below).

claim: The difference in performance between trained RNNs and exclusively motor trained RNNs confirms the importance of tuning recurrent weights to the sensory discrimination component.
source: The difference in performance between the trained RNNs (sensory and motor training) and the exclusively motor trained RNNs, confirms the importance of tuning the recurrent weights to the sensory discrimination component of the task (see below).

claim: RNNs operating in high-gain regimes are prone to chaotic behavior.
source: RNNs operating in high-gain regimes are prone to chaotic behavior (Sompolinsky et al., 1988; Rajan et al., 2010a) because the strong recurrent feedback of these networks rapidly amplifies any noise or perturbations.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work

claim: The RNN is operating in fundamentally different regimes during the sensory and motor epochs.
source: The distinction between epochs is critical since the RNN is operating in fundamentally different regimes during the sensory and motor epochs.
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: During the sensory epoch, recurrently generated internal dynamics are partially suppressed as a result of external input.
source: During the sensory epoch the recurrently generated internal dynamics are partially suppressed (or 'clamped') as a result of the external input
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: During the motor epoch, all activity is internally generated.
source: yet during the motor epoch all activity is internally generated.

claim: The motor trajectory briefly deviates from an unperturbed one after perturbation but recovers mid-voyage.
source: Figure 2A shows the activity of a hundred units from a trained RNN (and the resulting output), when it is presented with the digit 'three' and strongly perturbed (amplitude = 2) in the motor epoch. The resulting transcription briefly deviates from an unperturbed one (grey backdrop), but recovers mid-voyage.

claim: The sensory epoch is less sensitive to perturbations than the motor epoch.
source: The sensory epoch is less sensitive to perturbations—as would be expected because the presence of the external input serves as a stabilizing influence (Rajan et al., 2010a).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B-C with citation to prior work

claim: During the motor epoch, the RNN operates autonomously as a 'dynamic attractor' that can return to the original trajectory after perturbation.
source: During the motor epoch the RNN is operating autonomously as a 'dynamic attractor', that is, once bumped off its trajectory it maintains a memory of its current voyage and is able to return to the original trajectory (Laje and Buonomano, 2013) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B with citation to prior work

claim: Performance measurements reveal a graceful degradation across a wide range of perturbation magnitudes.
source: Performance measurements using the CNN classifier reveal a graceful degradation across a wide range of perturbation magnitudes, and confirm the superior robustness of the sensory epoch (Figure 2C).

claim: Firing rate traces of sample units in a trained RNN show more similar patterns of activity in response to different utterances of the same digit compared to a reservoir RNN.
source: Firing rate traces of sample units in a trained RNN show more similar patterns of activity in response to different utterances of the same digit, when compared to a reservoir RNN (Figure 3A–B).

claim: In the untrained network, trajectories produced by utterances of digits 'six' and 'eight' during the sensory epoch occupied a fairly large abutting volume of PCA subspace.
source: The trajectories produced in the untrained network by utterances of the digits 'six' and 'eight', during the sensory epoch, occupied a fairly large abutting volume of PCA subspace (Figure 3C)

claim: In the untrained network during the motor epoch, trajectories were highly variable because the network strongly and perpetually amplifies differences between utterances in a chaotic regime.
source: and during the motor epoch the trajectories were highly variable—the network strongly and perpetually amplifies the differences between utterances, because it is in a chaotic regime.

claim: In the trained RNN, sensory epoch trajectories of each digit were restricted to a narrower volume and better separated from other digits.
source: In contrast, in the trained RNN, sensory epoch trajectories of each digit were restricted to a narrower volume, and better separated from the volume representing the other digit (Figure 3D).

claim: During the motor epoch in trained RNNs, trajectories for different utterances of the same digit were constrained to a much narrower tube reflecting the dynamic attractor.
source: During the motor epoch, the trajectories for different utterances of the same digit were constrained to a much narrower tube—reflecting the dynamic attractor—and better separated from the motor trajectories of the other digit.

claim: The set of all within-digit trajectories can be thought of as populating a hypertube that delimits the volume of phase space traversed by the digit.
source: The set of all within-digit trajectories can be thought of as populating a hypertube that delimits the volume of phase space traversed by the digit.

claim: During the sensory epoch, the hypertube of trajectories represents a memory of a family of related spatiotemporal objects: the spoken digit.
source: During the sensory epoch, this hypertube of trajectories represents a memory of a family of related spatiotemporal objects: the spoken digit.

claim: During the motor epoch, the hypertube narrows to a dynamic attractor that represents the 'motor memory' of the corresponding handwritten digit.
source: During the motor epoch the network is autonomous, and the hypertube of all within-digit trajectories narrows to a dynamic attractor that represents the 'motor memory' of the corresponding handwritten digit.

claim: Cortical circuits undergo experience-dependent plasticity that results in optimization or specialization to tasks the animal is exposed to.
source: It is well established that cortical circuits undergo experience-dependent plasticity—a process that seems to result in the optimization or specialization of those circuits to the tasks the animal is exposed to (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Crist et al., 2001; Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Karmarkar and Dan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Training the RNN improves discrimination performance by tuning recurrent weights to the task at hand.
source: The above results establish that training the RNN does improve discrimination performance—the recurrent weights are tuned to the task at hand
evidence: Based on comparison of trained vs untrained network performance

claim: Training significantly decreases the mean within-digit distances during the sensory epoch.
source: Training significantly decreases the mean within-digit distances during the sensory epoch (Figure 4A).

claim: Training does not diminish the large separations between trajectories of different digits.
source: Importantly, in doing so, it does not diminish the large separations between trajectories of different digits.

claim: The same effect of decreased within-digit distance is observed during the motor epoch, much enhanced, as a consequence of dynamic attractor formation.
source: The same effect, much enhanced, is observed during the motor epoch, a consequence of the formation of dynamic attractors.

claim: Successful formation of dynamic attractors is strongly influenced by an unambiguous and stable sensory epoch-motor epoch transition.
source: Successful formation of these attractors is strongly influenced by an unambiguous and stable sensory epoch-motor epoch transition of the network dynamics.
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: A stable sensory-motor transition relies on low within-digit separation at the end of the sensory epoch trajectory.
source: Such a transition relies on two factors: (i) a low within-digit separation at the end of the sensory epoch trajectory, ensuring initial conditions at the beginning of the motor epoch that lie within the initial basin of attraction of the motor pattern-encoding dynamic attractor
evidence: Based on analysis of attractor dynamics

claim: A stable sensory-motor transition requires between-digit separation substantially larger than within-digit separation at the end of the sensory epoch.
source: (ii) a between-digit separation that is substantially larger than the within-digit separation of sensory epoch trajectories, particularly at the end of the sensory epoch, to ensure robust and divergent sensory-epoch-motor epoch transitions for different digits.
evidence: Based on analysis of attractor dynamics

claim: Training sculpts the dynamics of the RNN during the sensory epoch even though RNN activity is governed in part by external input.
source: The finding that training sculpts the dynamics of the RNN during the sensory epoch is also a critical one because it shows that even though RNN activity is governed in part by the external input, the internal connections are critical: tuning them effectively improves the interaction between the sensory input and the internally generated dynamics.
evidence: Based on analysis of within-digit and between-digit distances

claim: Training results in a collapsing of the family of trajectories representing a digit into a narrower hypertube.
source: This improvement is expressed as a collapsing of the family of trajectories representing a digit into a narrower hypertube.

claim: A single innate trajectory serves as a common target for different training utterances of a digit during supervised recurrent training.
source: These results follow as a direct consequence of the supervised recurrent training paradigm (Materials and Methods)—a single innate trajectory serves as a common target for different training utterances of a digit, thereby inducing changes in the network's recurrent dynamics that are necessary to encode the different utterances along similar neural trajectories

claim: Different digits are encoded in rapidly divergent trajectories because the target trajectories for each digit are generated by an untrained chaotic network.
source: However, different digits are encoded in rapidly divergent trajectories because the target trajectories for each digit are generated by an untrained chaotic network.

claim: Training results in a compression of eigenvalues with real part larger than one in the weight matrix eigenspectrum.
source: Training results in a compression of those eigenvalues with real part larger than one, bringing the maximal real part of the eigenvalues closer to one.

claim: The compression of the eigenspectrum is consistent with the increased stability of the network during the sensory and motor epochs.
source: nevertheless the compression of the eigenspectrum is consistent with the increased stability of the network during the sensory and motor epochs (Rajan and Abbott, 2006; Ostojic, 2014).

claim: Sensory discrimination requires circuits to be highly responsive to external stimuli to categorize inputs into discrete classes.
source: Sensory discrimination requires circuits to be highly responsive to external stimuli in order to categorize inputs into discrete classes.
evidence: Based on computational understanding of sensory processing

claim: Motor tasks require autonomous generation of spatiotemporal patterns and need network dynamics to be somewhat resistant to external inputs.
source: In contrast, motor tasks require autonomous generation of spatiotemporal patterns, and thus need the network dynamics to be somewhat resistant to external inputs.
evidence: Based on computational understanding of motor processing

claim: The balance between sensory and motor modes depends on the recurrent weights and the magnitude of the external drive.
source: In the network described here, this balance depends on the recurrent weights and the magnitude of the external drive.
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: The recurrent weights must be strong for the network to be in a high-gain regime.
source: The recurrent weights must be strong—that is the network must be in a high-gain regime—for two reasons.

claim: Network dynamics in high-gain regimes are high-dimensional, which naturally yields well-separated trajectories for different digits.
source: First, network dynamics in high-gain regimes are high-dimensional (Rajan et al., 2010b), which naturally yields well-separated trajectories for different digits.
evidence: Supported by citation with logical inference

claim: A network operating in a high-gain regime is inherently capable of generating the self-perpetuating activity required in the motor epoch.
source: Second, as noted earlier, a network operating in a high-gain regime is inherently capable of generating the self-perpetuating activity required in the motor epoch, which is then stabilized by the training procedure.
evidence: Based on properties of high-gain networks

claim: During the sensory epoch, the RNN operates in a regime that is both sensitive to external input and influenced by strong internal recurrent dynamics.
source: Thus during the sensory epoch, the RNN is operating in a regime that is both sensitive to external input and influenced by strong internal recurrent dynamics.
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: In the motor mode, the RNN operates autonomously, generating locally stable trajectories that serve as a high-dimensional 'engine' driving arbitrary low dimensional output patterns.
source: In the motor mode, the RNN operates autonomously, generating locally stable trajectories that serve as a high-dimensional 'engine' that drives arbitrary low dimensional output patterns.
evidence: Based on analysis of network dynamics

claim: The ability of the network to meaningfully process input patterns during the sensory epoch depends on the strength of the inputs.
source: The ability of the network to meaningfully process input patterns during the sensory epoch, so that they are easy to discriminate, also depends on the strength of the inputs.
evidence: Based on parametric analysis of input amplitude

claim: In the reservoir, both within and between-digit distances diminish as the input amplitude increases.
source: In the reservoir, both within and between-digit distances diminish as the input amplitude increases (Figure 5A, left panel), consistent with a previous study showing that strong inputs can progressively dominate and override the internal dynamics of an RNN (Rajan et al., 2010a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A with citation to prior work

claim: Input-dominated regimes effectively void the recurrent weights and render training useless.
source: In the extreme, input-dominated regimes effectively void the recurrent weights and render training useless (Figure 5A, right panel).

claim: At high input amplitudes, dimensionality measurements of sensory epoch trajectories mirror the low-dimensionality of the input cochleograms, regardless of training.
source: The poor discriminability at high input amplitudes is further confirmed by dimensionality measurements of sensory epoch trajectories (Materials and Methods), which mirror the low-dimensionality of the input cochleograms, regardless of training (Figure 5B).

claim: Low-input amplitude regimes are dominated by the RNN's internal dynamics.
source: In contrast, low-input amplitude regimes are dominated by the RNN's internal dynamics.
evidence: Based on analysis of input amplitude effects

claim: Reservoirs in low-input regimes produce chaotic high-dimensional dynamics and are insufficiently sensitive to external inputs.
source: Reservoirs in this regime produce chaotic high-dimensional dynamics and are insufficiently sensitivity to external inputs; thus the within- and between-digit distances are similarly high (Figure 5A, left).

claim: Training strongly alters the dynamics of low-input amplitude regimes, lowering dimensionality.
source: Training strongly alters these dynamics, lowering its dimensionality (Figure 5B).

claim: Trained RNNs in low-input regimes fail to improve discrimination due to poor input-sensitivity despite training-induced changes.
source: However, as a consequence of poor input-sensitivity, these changes fail to improve discrimination—trained RNNs in this regime still sustain similar within and between-digit distances (Figure 5B, right).

claim: RNNs trained at intermediate input amplitudes are both sensitive to the input and able to discriminate between digits.
source: RNNs trained at intermediate input amplitudes (0.5, 5) are both sensitive to the input and able to discriminate between digits, because their sensory epoch trajectories are shaped both by the input and internal dynamics.
evidence: Based on analysis across input amplitudes

claim: The input drive must be strong enough to influence ongoing activity but not strong enough to 'erase' recent information encoded in the current trajectory.
source: It is thus critical that the input drive be strong enough to influence ongoing activity but not strong enough to 'erase' recent information encoded in the current trajectory.
evidence: Based on analysis of input amplitude effects

claim: Spectral noise exhibits time-dependent structured relationships with the input signal.
source: First, spectral noise exhibits time-dependent structured relationships with the input signal (they may be correlated, anti-correlated or tend to occur along specific directions during specific parts of the input).
evidence: Based on analysis of spectral noise structure

claim: Spectral differences between utterances of one phoneme within a digit will be different than those of another.
source: For example, the spectral differences between utterances of one phoneme within a digit will be different than those of another.
evidence: Based on understanding of speech structure

claim: Invariance requires the network to isolate and integrate the signal while suppressing signal-dependent spectral noise.
source: Invariance then requires the network to isolate and integrate the signal while suppressing signal-dependent spectral noise.

claim: Spectral noise is a form of correlated noise delivered simultaneously to multiple recurrent units via common input projections.
source: Second, spectral noise is a form of correlated noise. The noise in each input channel is simultaneously delivered to multiple recurrent units via common input projections.

claim: Spectral noise is proportional in magnitude to the input amplitude and tends to be much stronger than background noise.
source: Third, spectral noise is proportional in magnitude to the input amplitude, and therefore tends to be much stronger than the background noise that is typically injected during training and testing.
evidence: Based on properties of spectral noise

claim: Measurements of within-digit trajectory distances revealed a progressive increase from trained utterances to untrained utterances to utterances with shuffled noise to utterances with orthogonal noise.
source: Measurements of the within-digit trajectory distances revealed a progressive increase from trained utterances, to untrained utterances, to utterances with shuffled noise, to utterances with orthogonal noise (Figure 6E).

claim: The untrained (reservoir) network exhibited deviations that were large and fairly similar across all conditions.
source: In contrast, the untrained (reservoir) network exhibited deviations that were large and fairly similar across all conditions, implying that the trained network was able to identify and suppress natural spectral noise present in the utterances, but not artificial noise of similar magnitude and structure.

claim: In untrained networks, both natural and artificial spectral noise introduced deviations in the recurrent subspace that were large and unsuppressed.
source: The analysis showed that in untrained networks, both natural and artificial spectral noise introduced deviations in the recurrent subspace that were large and unsuppressed (Figure 6F).

claim: In trained RNNs, the recurrent dynamics suppressed natural spectral noise but not artificial noise.
source: In contrast, in trained RNNs the recurrent dynamics suppressed natural spectral noise, but not artificial noise (Figure 6G).

claim: Training resulted in a recurrent subspace that suppressed spectral noise induced deviations in the input subspace.
source: Training also resulted in a recurrent subspace that suppressed spectral noise induced deviations in the input subspace.

claim: Training the network rotated the recurrent subspace such that spectral noise induced trajectory deviations in the recurrent subspace were anti-correlated with deviations in the input subspace.
source: Whereas the untrained network integrated recurrent and external inputs in orthogonal subspaces, training the network rotated the recurrent subspace such that spectral noise induced trajectory deviations in the recurrent subspace were anti-correlated with the deviations in the input subspace, thereby resulting in their suppression (Recurrent-Input interaction in Figure 6F–G).

claim: Recurrent plasticity may play a crucial role in identifying and suppressing the natural spatial variations of stimuli.
source: Together, these results suggest that recurrent plasticity may play a crucial role in identifying and suppressing the natural spatial variations of stimuli.
evidence: Based on analysis of spectral noise suppression

claim: Training shapes the basins of attraction around spoken digit-encoding trajectories based on the spatiotemporal distribution of spectral noise in the sensory input.
source: In our model, this is achieved via supervised training with a common within-digit target trajectory, which exposes the spatiotemporal distribution of the spectral noise in the sensory input, and in doing so, allows for effective sampling from this distribution. Training then shapes the basins of attraction or hypertubes around the spoken digit-encoding trajectories based on this distribution, resulting in effective, recurrently-driven suppression of naturally occurring spectral noise.

claim: Temporal warping (temporal invariance) is a signature and little understood feature of how the brain processes time-varying patterns.
source: As mentioned above, a signature and little understood feature of how the brain processes time-varying patterns pertains to temporal warping (temporal invariance), whereby temporally compressed or dilated input signals can be identified as the same pattern.

claim: One advantage of encoding time-varying stimuli as continuous neural trajectories is that it naturally addresses the problem of temporal warping.
source: We hypothesized that one advantage of encoding time-varying stimuli as continuous neural trajectories, is that it naturally addresses the problem of temporal warping; specifically, that compressed or dilated stimuli generate similar neural trajectories that play out at different 'speeds' (Lerner et al., 2014; Mello et al., 2015).

claim: Trajectories produced by temporally warped inputs in the sensorimotor trained RNN were closer to the reference compared to their counterparts in the reservoir or motor-trained RNN.
source: Trajectories produced by temporally warped inputs in the sensorimotor trained RNN were closer to the reference compared to their counterparts in the reservoir or motor-trained RNN.

claim: Tuning the recurrent weights dramatically improved the ability of the network to reproduce the same neural trajectories despite being driven by inputs at different speeds.
source: In other words, tuning the recurrent weights dramatically improved the ability of the network to reproduce the same neural trajectories, despite being driven by inputs at different speeds.
evidence: Based on comparison across network types

claim: The trained RNN maintains a much smaller distance between trajectories across a four-fold range of temporal warping including warp factors outside the range used during training.
source: In comparison to the two control networks, the trained RNN maintains a much smaller distance between trajectories across the four-fold range of temporal warping—including warp factors outside the range used during training.

claim: Training during the sensory and motor epochs dramatically improves extrapolation to speeds outside the range of training speeds.
source: Training during the sensory and motor epochs dramatically improves 'extrapolation'—that is generalization to speeds outside the range of training speeds

claim: Training during the motor epoch alone is sufficient to produce very good interpolation generalization to novel speeds within the training set range.
source: however, training during the motor epoch alone is sufficient to produce very good 'interpolation' (novel speeds within the training set range) generalization.

claim: A comparison of the time-averaged linear speed of trajectories encoding digits at different warps deviates from the inverse proportional relationship in both untrained and trained networks.
source: However, a comparison of the time-averaged linear speed of trajectories encoding digits at different warps deviates from this relationship in both the untrained and trained networks (Figure 8A)

claim: Temporal scaling is achieved by an approximate balance of constant speed and constant distance mechanisms.
source: A comparison of these measurements for the two networks to the expected values in constant speed- and constant distance trajectories, confirms that both networks produce trajectories that lie in between these two extremes.

claim: At low speeds (digits spoken slowly), the trajectories are slower and longer.
source: That is, temporal scaling is achieved by an approximate balance of both hypotheses, e.g., at low speeds (digits spoken slowly) the trajectories are slower and longer.
evidence: Based on analysis of trajectory speeds and distances

claim: Training alters the balance between constant speed and constant distance to reduce within-digit separation by modulating trajectory speeds more strongly.
source: Furthermore, training alters this balance to reduce the within-digit separation, by modulating the trajectory speeds more strongly.

claim: The input and recurrent subspaces in the trained network are orthogonal to one another.
source: To answer this question, we first measured the relationship between the input and recurrent subspaces in the trained network, and discovered that they are orthogonal to one another (data not shown)

claim: The differentiated curvature and linear velocity that modulate the angular velocity and timescales of recurrent subspace trajectories are directly shaped by input subspace dynamics.
source: Ultimately, the differentiated curvature and linear velocity that modulate the angular velocity and therefore the timescales of recurrent subspace trajectories, are directly shaped by these input subspace dynamics (Rajan et al., 2010a).

claim: A network trained with gradient-descent approach showed inferior interpolation and extrapolation performance compared to the network trained with 'innate' learning.
source: While the interpolation and extrapolation performance of this network was inferior to the network trained with 'innate' learning (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), the underlying mechanism was the same: warped utterances were encoded along parallel trajectories (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F–G) with warp-dependent curvature and linear velocity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2E) that subserved temporal scaling.

claim: Two very different training algorithms resulted in similar solutions to the temporal invariance problem.
source: Thus, two very different training algorithms resulted in similar solutions to the temporal invariance problem.
evidence: Comparison of innate learning and gradient descent approaches

claim: The integration of inputs at different warps separates out the resulting trajectories in the input subspace and consequently in the recurrent subspace.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that the integration of inputs at different warps separates out the resulting trajectories in the input subspace, and consequently in the recurrent subspace.

claim: The network dynamics generate trajectories with warp-dependent linear velocities and curvature which appropriately modulate their angular velocity.
source: In both subspaces the network dynamics generate trajectories with warp-dependent linear velocities and curvature, which appropriately modulate their angular velocity, resulting in them traversing spatially distinct yet parallel paths at warp-dependent timescales.

claim: An inherent computational advantage of encoding time-varying sensory stimuli in neural trajectories is that it can naturally address the temporal invariance problem.
source: This confirms the hypothesis that an inherent computational advantage of encoding time-varying sensory stimuli in neural trajectories is that it can naturally address the temporal invariance problem.
evidence: Conclusion based on temporal warping analysis

claim: Theoretical evidence increasingly suggests that the dynamics of recurrently connected circuits in the brain are critical to representing time-varying patterns.
source: Despite our poor understanding of these processes, theoretical evidence increasingly suggests that the dynamics of recurrently connected circuits in the brain are critical to representing time-varying patterns.

claim: Reservoir computing approaches propose that complex high-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns are represented in the dynamics inherent to randomly connected recurrent neural networks.
source: For example, so-called reservoir computing approaches propose that complex high-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns are represented in the dynamics inherent to randomly connected recurrent neural networks (Jaeger and Haas, 2004; Buonomano and Maass, 2009; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to reservoir computing literature

claim: A shortcoming of reservoir computing is that the recurrent connections are not plastic and do not adapt to the task at hand.
source: A shortcoming of this approach, however, is that the recurrent connections in these networks are not plastic; thus in contrast to actual cortical circuits, the random recurrent neural network (the 'reservoir') does not adapt or optimize to the task at hand.

claim: Fully tapping into the computational potential of randomly connected RNNs has proven difficult because they are susceptible to chaos.
source: Additionally, fully tapping into the computational potential of randomly connected RNNs has proven difficult because they are susceptible to chaos (Sompolinsky et al., 1988; Wallace et al., 2013).

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity could reshape the dynamics of reservoir RNNs to qualitatively improve representations by endowing them with generalization, sensory-motor association, and temporal invariance.
source: Here, we extend these results to better understand well-known aspects of the brain's ability to represent time-varying sensory and motor patterns—we demonstrate how experience-dependent plasticity could reshape the dynamics of reservoir RNNs to qualitatively improve representations by endowing them with such essential properties as generalization to novel exemplars, sensory-motor association and transformation, and temporal invariance.

claim: Previous models of temporal scaling have enlisted neural and synaptic dynamics to achieve temporal invariance of both sensory stimuli and motor responses.
source: Previous models of temporal scaling have enlisted neural and synaptic dynamics to achieve temporal invariance of both sensory stimuli (Gütig and Sompolinsky, 2009) and the generation of motor responses (Murray and Escola, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior models

claim: In the Gutig and Sompolinsky model, temporally invariant recognition is based on a synaptic shunting mechanism where the effective integration time is modulated by total conductance of afferent synapses.
source: In the model proposed by Gutig and Sompolinsky, temporally invariant recognition of compressed and dilated sensory stimuli is based on a synaptic shunting mechanism, wherein the effective integration time of a post-synaptic cell is modulated by the total conductance of its afferent synapses, which changes as a monotonic function of the input warp—thus temporal invariance is ultimately reduced to a cellular property.

claim: In the current model, temporal invariance emerges from a network property: the formation of parallel neural trajectories traversed at different speeds.
source: In contrast, in the model described here temporal invariance emerges from a network property: the formation of parallel neural trajectories traversed at different speeds.

claim: The capacity for parallel trajectories at different speeds is the consequence of scale-dependent angular velocities of the encoding trajectories.
source: While the formation of such trajectories may be surprising given the sensitivity and nonlinear nature of RNNs, we show that this capacity is the consequence of scale-dependent angular velocities of the encoding trajectories.

claim: The property of scale-dependent angular velocities stems from leaky integration of scaled inputs and input-driven suppression of chaotic recurrent activity.
source: This property of RNN encoding, which is observable to a lesser extent even in reservoir networks (Figure 8D), stems from its leaky integration of scaled inputs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and the input-driven suppression of its chaotic recurrent activity (Rajan et al., 2010a).
evidence: Explanation with figure references and citation

claim: Network training enhances scale-dependent angular velocities by suppressing recurrent amplification of scale-driven deviations in encoding trajectories.
source: Indeed, network training enhances this property by suppressing recurrent amplification of scale-driven deviations in the encoding trajectories, producing proximal, parallel within-digit trajectories with linear velocities that are more strongly scale-dependent (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1C, 2E and G).

claim: Training across both sensory and motor epochs improves interpolation and extrapolation generalization and strongly enhances cross-utterance and cross-speaker generalization.
source: Nevertheless, it remains the case that training across both the sensory and motor epochs, not only improves interpolation and extrapolation generalization, but also strongly enhances cross-utterance and cross-speaker generalization (Figure 1C).

claim: Training an RNN reveals a computationally powerful pattern recognition regime that helps generalize the encoding of learned time-varying patterns to novel exemplars.
source: Our results also demonstrate how training an RNN reveals a computationally powerful pattern recognition regime, one that helps generalize the encoding of learned time-varying patterns to novel exemplars.

claim: Recognizing different instances of the same digit as one and the same while discriminating between different digits requires networks to differentially sculpt within and between class trajectories.
source: As stated earlier, recognizing different instances of the same digit as one and the same, while discriminating between different digits requires that networks actively and differentially sculpt the within and between class trajectories—the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns must be kept to a minimum, while that between trajectories representing different patterns must be amplified.

claim: Untrained random recurrent networks (reservoir networks) in the critical regime amplify the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns more strongly than between different patterns.
source: A previous study has analytically shown that untrained random recurrent networks (reservoir networks) process inputs in one of three computational regimes: a chaotic regime, wherein any separation between trajectories is strongly amplified by the network's chaotic dynamics; a regime with weak recurrent weights that is input-dominated with little computational power; and a critical regime wherein the input and internal dynamics are balanced (Bertschinger and Natschläger, 2004). Here, we show that training alters these regimes in very different ways (Figure 5). Crucially, relative to the separation between the input patterns, reservoir networks in the critical regime amplify the separation between trajectories representing similar patterns more strongly than between different patterns.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5 with citation to prior work

claim: Trained networks separate trajectories according to the patterns they are representing.
source: In contrast, trained networks separate trajectories according to the patterns they are representing (Figure 5A).

claim: Tuning the recurrent weights reshapes the internal dynamics of the network, enabling it to redirect or suppress deviations from the target trajectories.
source: Tuning the recurrent weights reshapes the internal dynamics of the network, enabling it to redirect or suppress deviations from the target trajectories (Figure 6).

claim: The model predicts that neural trajectories will be stable in response to local perturbations potentially administered through optogenetic stimulation.
source: Three experimentally tractable predictions emerge from the above results. First, neural trajectories will be stable in response to local perturbations potentially administered through optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The model predicts that neural trajectories elicited during sensory stimuli will be more resistant to perturbations than neural trajectories during the motor epoch of sensory-motor tasks.
source: Importantly, and in agreement with an earlier analysis (Rajan et al., 2010a), the neural trajectories elicited during sensory stimuli will be more resistant to perturbations than the neural trajectories unfolding during the motor epoch of sensory-motor tasks.
evidence: Prediction based on model results with citation

claim: The model predicts that trajectories in sensory areas will diverge more when presented stimuli composed of artificial or unfamiliar spectral noise patterns.
source: A second prediction, which to the best of our knowledge is a novel one, relates to the structure of noise. Specifically, trained networks fail at generalizing to unfamiliar spectral noise patterns, thereby generating the prediction that trajectories in sensory areas will diverge more when presented stimuli composed of artificial or unfamiliar spectral noise patterns.
evidence: Prediction based on spectral noise analysis

claim: The model predicts that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii, implying neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in firing rates in response to slower stimuli.
source: Third, and most specifically, the model predicts a clear neural correlate of the encoding of temporally scaled stimuli—the observation that slower stimuli yield trajectories with larger curvature radii implies that the neural population activity should exhibit larger fluctuations in their firing rates in response to slower stimuli; In other words, at the neuronal level the range of minimal to maximal firing rate should be larger (Figure 8—figure supplements 1D and 2D).
evidence: Prediction based on trajectory analysis shown in figures

claim: The learning rule used in the model, coupled with its requirement of an explicit target for each recurrent unit, is biologically implausible.
source: Most notably, how can the recurrent synaptic strengths be tuned to develop stable trajectories in a biologically plausible manner? The learning rule used here, coupled with its requirement of an explicit target for each recurrent unit, make it biologically implausible.

claim: It is conceivable that arbitrary yet locally-stable encoding trajectories may emerge from unsupervised learning.
source: However, while it is important that the sensorimotor representations are encoded as locally stable trajectories, the structure of the target trajectories themselves are essentially arbitrary. It is therefore conceivable that arbitrary yet locally-stable encoding trajectories may emerge from unsupervised learning.

claim: It is not clear if training over a range of sensory stimuli speeds represents a biologically plausible scenario.
source: A second related issue is that to achieve strong temporal invariance, our model had to be trained over a range of sensory stimuli speeds. Again, it is not clear if this would represent a biologically plausible scenario

claim: It will be important for future research to determine if the ability to recognize stimuli independent of speed is learned through experience.
source: to help address this question, it will be important for future research to determine if the ability to recognize stimuli independent of speed is learned through experience.

claim: The computational potential of continuous time RNNs in high-gain regimes has long been recognized but has been challenging to tap into because of their inherently chaotic behavior and difficulties in training them.
source: The computational potential of continuous time RNNs in high-gain regimes has long been recognized, but it has been challenging to tap into this potential because of their inherently chaotic behavior and the difficulties in training them (Bengio et al., 1994; Pearlmutter, 1995).

claim: A further feature of trained RNNs is their ability to encode spatiotemporal objects, perform complex sensorimotor tasks, and address the problem of temporal warping.
source: Here, we establish that a further feature of trained RNNs is their ability to not only encode spatiotemporal objects, but also to perform complex sensorimotor tasks and address the long-standing problem of temporal warping.

claim: These results are consistent with the proposal that spatiotemporal objects are not encoded as fixed-point attractors but as locally stable neural trajectories (dynamic attractors).
source: These results are consistent with the proposal that that spatiotemporal objects are not encoded as fixed-point attractors, but as locally stable neural trajectories (dynamic attractors).
